one_liner: Growable, shrinkable cuckoo filter (linked cuckoo-filter blocks) with reliable deletes; beats a Dynamic Bloom Filter on space and speed.
what_it_does: DCF is an approximate-membership set for data whose size is unknown or changes over time. It starts as one cuckoo filter, links on identical cuckoo-filter blocks as it fills, and after deletions compact() moves fingerprints out of sparse blocks and unlinks the empty ones. A Dynamic Bloom Filter (a chain of counting Bloom filters) skips a delete whenever more than one block matches. DCF gives each item its own fingerprint, so a delete always removes exactly one entry. The API is a research class, not a packaged library: new DynamicCuckooFilter(max_items, target_fpr, expected_blocks = 6), then insertItem / queryItem / deleteItem on NUL-terminated const char* keys, plus compact().
how_it_is_fast: Each block is a standard Fan et al. cuckoo filter: 4-slot buckets, partial-key cuckoo hashing (alternate bucket = index XOR hash(fingerprint)) and up to 500 kicks. When a block reaches 93.75% load, a new block with the same table length and hash is linked on. A victim left over from a failed insert goes to the same bucket index in the next block. A lookup checks the 4 packed fingerprints of a bucket at once with SWAR 'hasvalue' bit tricks (Stanford bithacks haszero4/8/12/16), so each block costs 2 bucket probes, where each DBF block costs k 4-bit counter reads. A DCF delete stops at the first matching block; the in-repo DBF scans every block twice. Compaction is greedy: it moves fingerprints from the sparsest block into the same bucket indexes of denser blocks.
when_to_use: You need an approximate set that must both grow and shrink with a fluctuating or unknown item count, and also support deletes. An example is the in-memory chunk-fingerprint index for deduplication in the paper's file-backup prototype.

You are replacing a Dynamic Bloom Filter or a chain of counting Bloom filters where deletes get skipped when several blocks match. Here each item owns one fingerprint, so deletes are exact for inserted items.
FPR targets are moderate (about 1e-2 down to 5e-4 with the default ~6 blocks), so 16-bit or smaller fingerprints are enough, and the final item count stays close to the planned maximum.
You want a short (~850 lines), readable reference for the ICNP 2017 design to port into your own codebase with a fast non-cryptographic hash and proper memory management.
when_not_to_use: Capacity is known up front. A single fixed-size cuckoo, xor or binary fuse filter avoids the per-block probing, and query and delete time here grows linearly with the number of blocks (paper Fig. 13 and 15).

The filter grows well past its planned size or serves many negative lookups. Every miss probes 2 buckets in every block, and FPR compounds per block: open issue #2 reports FPR approaching 100% after growing from 1,000 to 30,000 items at a 3% per-block target.
FPR targets below about 5e-4 at the default settings. Fingerprints are capped at 16 bits: any computed size from 17 to 32 bits is silently set to 16, so the target is not met.

Anything production-facing. SHA-1 is computed only over the first sizeof(const char*) bytes of the key, destructors double-free, compact() leaks and can cause false negatives, and the repo has been unmaintained since 2017.
Concurrent access. There is no synchronization, and kick-out victims are chosen with the global rand().

integration.dependencies: OpenSSL libcrypto (SHA-1 through the EVP API; the makefile links -lssl -lcrypto)
integration.min_toolchain: C++98-style g++ code (no C++11 features). It needs the OpenSSL 1.0.x EVP API: a stack-allocated EVP_MD_CTX and EVP_MD_CTX_cleanup. OpenSSL 1.1.0 made these structures opaque (EVP_MD_CTX_new/free), so OpenSSL 1.1 and 3.x need a small patch.
integration.platforms: Tested only on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 14.04). The code assumes little-endian layout and uses unaligned, type-punned integer loads on the bucket bytes.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. There is no locking, and the shared Victim member and global rand() mean it is single-threaded only.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it has the same constructor signature and insertItem/queryItem/deleteItem(const char*) calls as the repo's own DynamicBloomFilter class (the two test harnesses differ only in the class name), plus compact(). It is not a drop-in for any external Bloom filter library.

gotchas: Hashing bug: HashFunc::sha1 hashes sizeof(key) bytes, where key is a const char*, so 8 bytes on 64-bit. Keys that share an 8-byte prefix always collide. Keys shorter than 7 characters hash bytes past their NUL terminator, so the same key stored in different buffers can hash differently, which means false negatives. The bundled benchmark hides this by reusing the same string buffers for insert, query and delete.

Memory handling is broken. ~CuckooFilter deletes both next and front, so linked blocks free each other twice. ~DynamicCuckooFilter deletes curCF and then the list head, which is the same pointer. LinkList::remove() unlinks a block during compact() but never frees it and never fixes tail_pt, the successor's front pointer or curCF. After the README's delete-everything-then-compact flow the block count is 0, so every later insert lands in an unlinked block and is never found. Open issue #3 reports a segfault (no details).

The reported space_cost (size_in_mb) counts fingerprint bits only. Each 8-byte bucket is a separate new char[] allocation plus an 8-byte pointer, so real heap use is at least 2x the reported figure before allocator overhead. The constructor also leaks 3 preallocated blocks. For 4/8/12-bit fingerprints, queryImpl reads 8 bytes from buckets allocated as 2/4/6 bytes, which is a heap over-read.

The build instructions are wrong. The README says 'cd src/; make test', but the makefile is at the repo root and uses src/ paths, and the test binary reads ./configuration/config.txt and writes ./result/result.txt relative to the working directory. makefile_DBF points at src/*.cpp although the DBF sources live in src_DBF/, so the baseline does not build as shipped.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick DCF over efficient/cuckoofilter, Vacuum Filter or Morton Filter only when the set must grow and later shrink with reliable deletes; those are fixed-capacity cuckoo-style filters. Its same-lab successor E2CF instead grows at the bucket-entry level to avoid probing many blocks, and reports up to 82% lower query time than existing designs. Prefer E2CF when lookups dominate.
verified_claims_summary: One README run inserts, queries and deletes 1M decimal-integer strings at a 0.0005 FPR target. The baseline is the repo's own Dynamic Bloom Filter, built from 4-bit counting Bloom filters. Both are compiled with g++ -Wall at default -O0, timed with clock() on an i5-2430M under Ubuntu 14.04, with SHA-1 per operation on both sides. DCF takes 1.08/1.05/1.36 s for insert/query/delete versus 1.69/1.92/3.35 s for DBF. DCF computes 2.5 MB of fingerprint bits versus 10.88 MB of DBF counter bits; this is not measured heap, and about 4x of that gap comes from the counters, since plain 1-bit Bloom arrays would be roughly 2.7 MB. The ICNP 2017 paper reports similar gains at FPR 1.17e-2 with up to 64,512 items: about 50% faster insert, 80% faster query, 25% faster delete and 75% less memory.
status_note: Abandoned since November 2017, with issues on FPR degradation and a segfault left unanswered. It is Apache-2.0 and about 850 lines, so treat it as a reference implementation of the ICNP 2017 design to port and fix (OpenSSL 1.0-era hashing, destructors, compaction) rather than a library to link.
